subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Cygnus X-1: The First Black Hole Candidate
description: One-minute skill: Cygnus X-1: The First Black Hole Candidate.

hook.text: Cygnus X-1 was the first object widely accepted as a black hole. The evidence built over decades of debate.

buildup.text: Discovered in 1964, it's an X-ray source 6,000 light-years away. A 21-solar-mass black hole orbits a blue supergiant.

discovery.text: Gas stripped from the companion star heats to millions of degrees, producing intense X-rays as it spirals inward.

twist.text: Stephen Hawking famously bet against it being a black hole in 1974. He conceded in 1990 after mounting evidence.

climax.text: In 2021, new measurements confirmed Cygnus X-1 is even more massive than thought—21 solar masses, not 15.

punchline.text: Decades of doubt, then certainty. The first black hole we believed in.

quiz.question: Why did it take decades to confirm Cygnus X-1 as a black hole?
options: Direct evidence was hard to obtain, and the concept itself was still debated
It was too far away for early telescopes to observe
Scientists believed it was a neutron star until the 2000s

details.summary: Cygnus X-1, discovered as a bright X-ray source in 1964, became the first widely accepted stellar-mass black hole candidate. Its companion star's orbital motion revealed an invisible object of about 21 solar masses — far above the neutron star limit.
details.whyItMatters: Cygnus X-1 transformed black holes from theoretical curiosities into observed reality. Its identification as a likely black hole in the 1970s was a pivotal moment in astrophysics.
takeaways: First widely accepted black hole candidate, discovered in 1964
About 21 solar masses — far above neutron star limits
Featured in a famous bet between Hawking and Thorne

faq.question: What was the Hawking-Thorne bet about Cygnus X-1?
faq.answer: In 1975, Hawking bet Thorne that Cygnus X-1 was NOT a black hole — as 'insurance' so that even if black holes didn't exist, he'd win something. By 1990, evidence was overwhelming, and Hawking conceded, signing the bet with his thumbprint and paying with a magazine subscription.

faq.question: How do we know Cygnus X-1 is a black hole?
faq.answer: Its companion star's orbital motion reveals the invisible object's mass at about 21 solar masses — far exceeding the neutron star maximum of about 2.5 solar masses. Its X-ray emission properties match accretion disk models for black holes. No known object other than a black hole fits.
